evidence.claim: Tunkhannock Creek ends its 42.3-mile course at the Susquehanna in Tunkhannock.
evidence.quote: Tunkhannock Creek is a 42.3-mile-long (68.1 km) tributary of the Susquehanna River in Northeastern Pennsylvania.

evidence.claim: Tunkhannock Creek ends its 42.3-mile course at the Susquehanna in Tunkhannock.

evidence.claim: Its source is Cheraine Pond near Jackson, and its branches gather water from Herrick Township and from near Montdale in Scott Township.
evidence.quote: Tunkhannock Creek is traced northeast along PA Highway 92 to its source of Cheraine Pond near Jackson. It has an eastern branch that rises in Herrick Township to the east and north of Elk Mountain and a southern branch that rises near Montdale in Scott Township.

evidence.claim: Upstream near Nicholson, the creek passes beneath the multiple concrete arches of the 2,400-foot Tunkhannock Viaduct, locally called the Nicholson Bridge.
evidence.quote: The 2,400-foot-long (730 m) Erie Lackawanna Railway Tunkhannock Viaduct (called locally the "Nicholson Bridge"), featuring multiple high concrete arches, passes over the creek near Nicholson.

flags: Overview is shorter because the cache gives little road character or construction history. Designation chronology is documented; no causal connection to historic-district designation is claimed.
Visit Pennsylvania loosely says US 6; PennDOT specifies Business Route 6. The story follows the more precise designation and does not put the byway on the bypass.
No strip towns supplied. Moments are ordered west to east by cached coordinates; the creek and mountain are separate geographic subjects, not verified driving stops or public-access promises.
The creek entry describes the Nicholson viaduct as upstream, not within this short byway. Cache has no confluence access instructions.
Osterhout Mountain is short because its cache contains only location and summit-tower facts. No summit access is asserted.
Tunkhannock name translations differ between town and creek pages, which also use Minsi-Len’api and Lenni-Lenape respectively. Etymology and nation terminology omitted pending a community source.
No unsupported current historical claims were found; the forty-two-mile rounding is replaced with the cached 42.3 miles.
The creek moment is shorter than 90 words because additional cached material is mostly distances, tributary names and unresolved etymology; it does not establish a viewpoint or visitor access.
